fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. The burnt offering stays on the altar's hearth all night, and the fire has to keep burning the whole time. Verse 13 comes back to it: "The fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it must not be extinguished." Every morning the priest adds wood to that fire (Leviticus 6:12). So the fire stays lit, night and morning.

Nice try, but lighting it fresh would mean the fire went out first, and verse 12 says it "must not be extinguished." What the priest does each morning is add wood to the fire that's already burning. I'd love to watch someone try to relight a fire that never went out, though. Spoiler: it's already going, friend.

That's the word, baker. After the handful goes up on the altar, the rest is for Aaron and his sons to eat. The text says it's eaten without leaven, in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Verse 17 calls it their portion of God's food offerings, so the leftovers go to the priests by God's own assignment.

No price tag and no clearance rack here, friend. Verse 16 says Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder, and verse 17 calls it their portion of God's food offerings. The instruction is to eat it without leaven, in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Selling never comes up.

Yes, baker. Verse 23 gives the rule: every grain offering for a priest is burned completely, and none of it is eaten. That's different from the grain offering in verses 14 to 16, where Aaron and his sons eat the remainder. So the priests eat from that one, but a grain offering for a priest goes up in full. Nothing left over, and no plate.

Right, baker. The priest who offers the sin offering is the one who eats it. Verse 26 says it must be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. The text calls it most holy, so this is serious business. I'd treat every bite with respect.

Right, friend. A clay pot used to boil the sin offering must be broken. If it's boiled in a bronze pot instead, that pot must be scoured and rinsed with water (Leviticus 6:28). Two kinds of pot, two instructions. I've dropped a pan or two in my day, but this is the one time breaking a pot is the instructions.

No pot handoff in this verse, friend. Verse 28 says a clay pot used to boil the sin offering must be broken. A bronze pot gets scoured and rinsed with water instead. Giving the pot to the priest isn't in there.

That's it, baker. Verse 7 says "The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both." Both are most holy, both are slaughtered where the burnt offering is slaughtered, and males among the priests may eat them in a holy place. There's one exception for the sin offering: if its blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place, it must be burned (Leviticus 6:30).

Yes, baker. An unclean person who eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD must be cut off from his people. Verse 21 says the same about someone who touches something unclean and then eats the meat. This is a heavy part of the passage. I think it's one to read slowly.

The elders aren't mentioned here, friend. Verse 23 says the LORD tells Moses, "Speak to the Israelites and say…" So the fat command is for all the Israelites. The elders don't come up in these verses.

You've got it, baker. The fat goes up on the altar, and the breast is for Aaron and his sons. Verse 30 says the one presenting the offering brings it with his own hands and waves the breast as a wave offering before the LORD. Verse 34 calls the breast a permanent portion for the priests.

The Passover isn't mentioned in these verses, friend. Verse 38 says the LORD gave Moses these laws on Mount Sinai, on the day He commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai. That's the command the verse names for that day. Keeping the Passover feast isn't part of it.
